dateConvention: Dates are Julian (Old Style) throughout, the calendar Georgia and Russia kept. From about 1490 Georgia was split into Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti; the deck follows the eastern kingdoms, with grouped cards for the stretches of Mongol, Timurid, Ottoman and Persian overlordship.
epilogue: In 1801 Russia annexed Kartli-Kakheti, ending a thousand years of Bagrationi rule in the east; the royal family was taken to Russia and Imereti followed in 1810. Georgia was free again in 1918–21 and since 1991.

reigns.tagline: The borderland prince who started a thousand-year dynasty
reigns.previously: Colchis, Iberia, a saint named Nino, then Persians and Arab emirs.
paragraphs: Long before the Bagrationi, Georgia was two lands. In the west lay Colchis, where Greek myth put the Golden Fleece. In the east lay Iberia, which Georgians call Kartli. In the 4th century its king, Mirian III, became a Christian through the preaching of Nino, a woman from Cappadocia. The Persians abolished the Iberian crown around 580, and from the 7th century Arab emirs sat in Tbilisi.

Ashot belonged to the Bagrationi, a family whose lands lay in Tao-Klarjeti, the rugged south-west where Byzantium and the caliphate met. Around 813 he became presiding prince of Iberia, the first of his family to hold the job. Constantinople gave him the grand court title kuropalates. He built up the fortress of Artanuji and backed the monk Grigol of Khandzta, who filled the valleys of Klarjeti with monasteries.

On 29 January 826 Ashot was murdered. Who killed him, and why, is far from clear. The Georgian Church later made him a saint. His sons divided his lands, and the Bagrationi kept growing, branch by branch.

claims.text: The Bagrationi were descended from King David of Israel.
claims.note: A family tradition first written down in the 11th century by the chronicler Sumbat Davitis-dze. It gave the kings a biblical pedigree; historians treat it as legend.

claims.text: Nino converted Iberia carrying a cross of vine branches bound with her own hair.
claims.note: The conversion of King Mirian is real history. The details of Nino's life come from Church texts written down centuries later.

claims.text: Ashot built Artanuji as his stronghold.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicles credit him with it, but how much he founded and how much he simply rebuilt is unclear.

reigns.hook: Ashot's sons carve up his lands. For sixty years nobody calls himself king of the Georgians. Then one of his great-grandsons decides the time has come.

reigns.tagline: The crown comes back after three hundred years
reigns.cameToPower: Beat his rival Nasra in battle
reigns.previously: Ashot I is murdered. His sons split Tao-Klarjeti between them.
paragraphs: After Ashot, the Bagrationi lands were shared out among his sons and grandsons, each branch with its own corner of Tao-Klarjeti. They quarrelled, but they also prospered. In 881 a cousin, Nasra, murdered Adarnase's father, and Adarnase, Ashot's great-grandson, became duke of Lower Tao.

Nasra fled to Constantinople and came back in 888 with Byzantine backing. Adarnase beat him and took a title no one had held for about three hundred years: King of the Iberians. Byzantium made him kuropalates in 891. He was one power among several. Kings of Abkhazia ruled the west, an Arab emir still held Tbilisi, and the Bagratid kings of Armenia watched from the south.
His kingdom was more a title than a state, but the title mattered. When Adarnase died in 923, the Bagrationi had a crown again, and they never let go of it.

claims.text: Adarnase was the first king in Kartli for about three centuries.
claims.note: The old Iberian monarchy ended around 580. Toumanoff and later historians date the revival of the royal title to 888.

claims.text: Nasra had the empire behind him.
claims.note: The sources for these years are thin. How much real help Byzantium gave Nasra is unclear.

reigns.hook: After Adarnase, the royal title passes around a quarrelsome family. The man who sets the Georgian lands on the road to unity is a prince of Tao: David III, the Great Kuropalates.

reigns.tagline: The kingmaker of Tao who willed his land to an emperor
reigns.previously: Adarnase IV dies in 923. The crown survives, but power is scattered.
paragraphs: Forty years after Adarnase, the real power in Georgian lands sat in Tao, the Bagrationi homeland on the Byzantine border. Its prince, David III, was a cousin of the royal line. On paper the King of the Iberians was his kinsman Bagrat II, known as “the Simple”, who held that title from 958 to 994. In practice, everyone looked to David. Byzantium made him kuropalates, one of its highest court ranks.

In 979 the emperor Basil II needed help against the rebel general Bardas Skleros. David sent his army, it helped win the decisive battle, and Basil paid him in land. Then David backed the wrong rebel. He supported Bardas Phokas in 987, and when that revolt collapsed he had to name Basil heir to Tao. At Oshki he built a great church and had himself carved on its walls.

Childless, David adopted a young kinsman, Bagrat, son of Gurgen, and set him up in Kartli in 975. Three years later the boy also became King of Abkhazia through his mother's family. David was murdered in 1000 or 1001, and Basil II marched in at once to take Tao for the empire.

claims.text: David was poisoned in the Communion cup by a churchman, at the urging of nobles in the emperor's pay.
claims.note: The Armenian historian Aristakes Lastivertsi tells it this way. No other source can confirm the plot.

claims.text: The great church at Oshki was built for David between about 963 and 973.
claims.note: Inscriptions on the church give the building period, but scholars read the exact years differently.

claims.text: David's troops helped Basil II defeat Bardas Skleros in 979.
claims.note: Byzantine and Georgian sources both record the Georgian army's part in the decisive battle.

reigns.hook: David is dead and Tao is Byzantine. In Kartli, Bagrat's father Gurgen still wears the old royal title, and he has his eye on what David left behind.

reigns.tagline: The father who kept the throne warm for his son
reigns.cameToPower: King of Kings of the Iberians from 994
reigns.previously: David of Tao is murdered, and Basil II marches in to take Tao.
paragraphs: Gurgen was a Bagrationi too, the son of Bagrat II the Simple, the old King of the Iberians. When his father died in 994, Gurgen took an even grander style: King of Kings of the Iberians. His son outshone him all the same. Bagrat, the boy David of Tao had adopted, was already King of Abkhazia in the west and master of Kartli in the east.

When David was murdered in 1000, Gurgen saw a chance. He led an army towards Tao, hoping to grab some of the dead prince's lands before the emperor could. Basil II's men turned him back. Gurgen made his peace with Byzantium, and got a court title instead of land.
For eight more years father and son held the Georgian lands between them. Then in 1008 Gurgen died, and everything he had passed to Bagrat.

claims.text: Gurgen's attempt to seize Tao was beaten off by Byzantine troops.
claims.note: Byzantine and Georgian accounts agree he failed, but give few details of the fighting or who led the imperial side.

claims.text: Gurgen took the style King of Kings of the Iberians after his father's death in 994.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle and modern historians such as Toumanoff give him this title.

reigns.hook: Gurgen is dead. His son Bagrat now holds the west, Kartli and his father's crown. For the first time, one man can call himself king of the Georgians, east and west.

reigns.tagline: East meets west, and Georgia becomes one kingdom
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Gurgen; heir of David of Tao
reigns.previously: Gurgen dies in 1008, and his son Bagrat gets it all.
paragraphs: Bagrat had been King of Abkhazia, ruling the west, since 978. When his father Gurgen died in 1008, he inherited Kartli too. For the first time, east and west answered to one crown, and his title said so: King of the Abkhazians and Georgians. Georgians call him Bagrat the Unifier, and they date their kingdom from him.

He kept going. Around 1010 he took Kakheti and Hereti in the east. At Kutaisi, his western capital, he raised the great Bagrati Cathedral. He was ruthless with his own family. The Bagrationi princes of Klarjeti were invited to a meeting with him and found themselves in prison, and their line died out there.
Bagrat died in Tao on 7 May 1014. He left a young son, George, and a kingdom that had only just been stitched together.

claims.text: Bagrat lured his Klarjeti cousins to a meeting and let their families die in prison.
claims.note: Only the Georgian chronicle tells it, and it presents the deed as harsh but needed for unity.

claims.text: An inscription dates the floor of the Bagrati Cathedral to 1003.
claims.note: The date is set into the building itself, five years before Bagrat ruled all Georgia.

claims.text: Bagrat was the first king of a united Georgia.
claims.note: Kartli and Abkhazia were joined under him in 1008. Tao and some other Georgian lands still lay outside.

reigns.hook: George inherits a big new kingdom and an old grudge. Tao, the family homeland, is in Byzantine hands, and he wants it back.

reigns.tagline: He picked a fight with Basil II and paid with his son
reigns.previously: Bagrat the Unifier dies, leaving one Georgia to his young son.
paragraphs: George, Giorgi in Georgian, was still a boy when he became king, and he wanted Tao, the old Bagrationi homeland that Byzantium took after David of Tao died. While Basil II was busy grinding down Bulgaria, George's men moved into the disputed lands.

Basil finished with Bulgaria and came east. In 1021 he beat George in a bloody battle near Shirimni, and in 1022 he returned to finish the job. The peace cost George border lands and his three-year-old son Bagrat, who went to Constantinople as a hostage.
He got the boy back, but not the lands. George died on 16 August 1027, still a young man, and the crown passed to Bagrat, aged nine.

claims.text: Little Bagrat was held in Constantinople for three years.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle gives three years. Other sources are vaguer about how long he stayed.

claims.text: Basil II beat George near Shirimni in 1021.
claims.note: Recorded by Byzantine historians, including Skylitzes, and by the Georgian chronicle.

reigns.hook: Georgia's new king is nine and has already been a hostage. The great nobles smell weakness, and one of them, Liparit, smells his chance.

reigns.tagline: Forty-five years of rebel nobles, emperors and Turks
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a boy
reigns.previously: George I dies young. His son Bagrat, once a hostage, is just nine.
paragraphs: Bagrat became king at nine, with his mother Mariam, a princess of Vaspurakan in Armenia, as regent. His reign became a long tug of war with Liparit Orbeli, the mightiest noble in the land. Liparit had Byzantine backing, and at one point he drove Bagrat out of his own kingdom. In the 1050s Bagrat spent about three years at the Byzantine court, working to win the emperor round.

Then a new danger rode in from the east. The Seljuk Turks were sweeping across Iran, and in 1068 their sultan Alp Arslan ravaged Georgia. That same year Bagrat took Tbilisi from its emir, but he couldn't keep it.

His daughter Maria, known as Maria of Alania, married two Byzantine emperors in turn, Michael VII and Nikephoros III. Bagrat died on 24 November 1072, leaving his son George a kingdom in the path of the Turks.

claims.text: Bagrat spent about three years at the Byzantine court in the 1050s.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle tells of the stay; historians disagree on the exact years.

claims.text: Maria of Alania was the great beauty of the Byzantine court.
claims.note: Anna Komnene, who knew her, praised her beauty at length in the Alexiad.

reigns.hook: Bagrat's son inherits a kingdom with the Turks already through the door. What comes next, Georgians will remember as the Great Turkish Troubles.

reigns.tagline: The king pushed aside for his own teenage son
reigns.previously: Bagrat IV dies with the Seljuk Turks pressing in.
paragraphs: George II had the bad luck to rule just as the Seljuks hit their peak. In 1071 they smashed the Byzantine army at Manzikert, and the empire's shield over the Caucasus was gone. From about 1080 Turkish nomads poured into Georgia, burning villages and grazing their herds on Georgian fields. Georgians call it the Didi Turkoba, the Great Turkish Troubles.
George couldn't stop them. He paid tribute, and he went to the sultan Malik Shah to submit in person, coming home with his throne and a bill. The nobles lost patience.
In 1089 they made him crown his 16-year-old son David as king. George kept the name of co-king, but the power had passed to the boy. He lived on until 1112.

claims.text: George travelled to Isfahan to kneel before Malik Shah.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle tells of the journey, but the date, place and terms are uncertain.

claims.text: Turkish nomads overran Georgia from about 1080.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle describes the raids in grim detail, and Armenian writers record the same wave.

reigns.hook: The new king is sixteen. His kingdom pays tribute, his nobles are restless and the Turks are everywhere. Georgians will one day call him the Builder.

reigns.tagline: The teenage king who built Georgia's golden age
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned when nobles sidelined his father
reigns.previously: George II is pushed aside. His son David, aged 16, is king.
paragraphs: David, Davit in Georgian, took over a kingdom that paid tribute to the Turks, and he went straight to work. In the 1090s he stopped paying, helped by the First Crusade, which kept the Turks busy further west. In 1103 a Church council at Ruisi-Urbnisi cleared out bishops he couldn't trust. He settled Kipchak warriors from the steppe in Georgia, married a Kipchak princess, and built a standing army.

On 12 August 1121, at Didgori, he met a much larger Seljuk coalition led by Ilghazi. The Georgians won so completely that they still call it the miraculous victory, and celebrate it every August. In 1122 David took Tbilisi, ending some four hundred years of Muslim rule there, and made it his capital. After a first day of plunder, he left its Muslims free to worship.

In 1106 he had founded the Gelati monastery near Kutaisi, with an academy for scholars. He died on 24 January 1125 and was buried there. His son Demetrius took over the strongest kingdom in the Caucasus.

claims.text: David asked to be buried under Gelati's gate so that every visitor would step on him.
claims.note: A tradition told to explain his tomb slab, which lies in the south gateway. His own wishes aren't recorded in the chronicle.

claims.text: David settled 40,000 Kipchak families in Georgia.
claims.note: The figure comes from his Georgian biographer. Historians think it may be inflated.

claims.text: David went to the mosque in Tbilisi and treated Muslims with respect.
claims.note: Told by later Muslim historians, such as Badr al-Din al-Ayni in the 15th century, drawing on earlier writers. They also say the city was plundered on the first day.

reigns.hook: David leaves his son a great kingdom with great enemies. Demetrius will hold it, raid beyond it and write hymns. His hardest fight will be with his own son.

reigns.tagline: Warrior, poet, and a father deposed by his son
reigns.previously: David the Builder dies, master of Tbilisi and the Caucasus.
paragraphs: Demetrius, Demetre in Georgian, spent his reign holding on to what his father had won. He fought off the Turkish emirs to the south, and in 1139 he raided the city of Ganja. His men carried its iron gate all the way home to Gelati as a trophy. It is still there, Arabic inscription and all.

He was a poet too. Georgians still sing a hymn, Thou Art a Vineyard, that tradition says he wrote. His family was harder to manage than his enemies. In 1154 his son David rebelled and forced him to give up the throne. David V lasted only a few months and died in 1155.
Demetrius came back and made his younger son George his heir, passing over David's son Demna. He died in 1156. The question of Demna would not go away.

claims.text: The iron gate of Ganja still stands at Gelati.
claims.note: The gate survives at the monastery with its Arabic inscription, and the Georgian chronicle records the raid.

claims.text: Demetrius wrote the hymn Thou Art a Vineyard.
claims.note: Georgian tradition credits him, but his authorship can't be proven.

claims.text: David V was poisoned.
claims.note: The chronicles hint at it without naming anyone. He may simply have fallen ill.

reigns.hook: George III takes the throne. His nephew Demna, the son of David V, thinks it should be his, and the great nobles are listening.

reigns.tagline: The iron-fisted king who crowned his daughter
reigns.previously: Demetrius I dies. His younger son is king; his grandson Demna waits.
paragraphs: George III was a fighter. In 1161 he took the old Armenian capital of Ani from the Shaddadid emirs, and his armies raided deep into Persia. The Bagrationi kingdom was now a name to fear across the region.

In 1177 the great nobles rose for Demna, son of David V, whom many saw as the rightful king. George crushed them. Demna was blinded and castrated, and the Orbeli family, leaders of the revolt, were wiped out. Nobody tried that again while George lived.

George had no son, only a daughter, Tamar. In 1178 he crowned her as his co-ruler, so that nobody could deny her the throne. He died on 27 March 1184, and for the first time a woman ruled Georgia in her own right.

claims.text: George had his nephew Demna blinded and castrated.
claims.note: Georgian and Armenian writers both report it. The details, and what became of Demna afterwards, are less certain.

claims.text: The Orbeli family was destroyed after the revolt of 1177.
claims.note: The outline is told in both Georgian and Armenian sources; the Orbelis vanish from Georgian power after it.

claims.text: George crowned Tamar co-ruler in 1178.
claims.note: The chronicles record it, and the two appear together in the wall paintings at Vardzia.

reigns.hook: Tamar is young, a woman on a throne built for warriors. The nobles and the Church think she'll be easy to manage. They are wrong.

reigns.tagline: The queen they called king
reigns.previously: George III dies. His daughter Tamar is already crowned and waiting.
paragraphs: Georgian sources call Tamar mepe, king, not queen. She was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right, and at first the nobles and the Church tried to rein her in. They found her a husband, Yury, a Rus' prince and son of Andrey Bogolyubsky. After about two years she divorced him and sent him away. He came back twice with armies and was beaten both times.

Her second husband, David Soslan, was an Ossetian prince and a fine general. Georgian armies won at Shamkor in 1195 and at Basian a few years later. In 1204 Tamar helped her relatives Alexios and David Komnenos set up the Empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea coast.

This was Georgia's golden age. Monks carved the cave monastery of Vardzia, where her portrait still looks down from the wall. Shota Rustaveli dedicated his epic, The Knight in the Panther's Skin, to her. She died on 18 January 1213, and her son George took over.

claims.text: Rustaveli was in love with Tamar.
claims.note: The poem's prologue praises Tamar, which is certain. Almost nothing is known about Rustaveli himself, and the love story is later legend.

claims.text: Tamar's grave was hidden on purpose so enemies could never find it.
claims.note: Nobody knows where she lies. Traditions point to Gelati or even to the Holy Land; the secrecy story grew up later.

claims.text: The Battle of Basian was fought in 1202.
claims.note: Sources and historians date it anywhere from 1202 to 1205.

reigns.hook: Tamar's son George, nicknamed Lasha, inherits the golden age. He is young, charming and fond of a party. Far to the east, the Mongols are on the move.

reigns.previously: Tamar the Great dies in 1213, leaving Georgia at its height.
paragraphs: Giorgi was the son of Queen Tamar and her second husband, the Ossetian prince David Soslan. He had been crowned co-king in 1207, so nobody argued when he took over. Everyone called him Lasha, a nickname said to mean “bright”. He inherited the richest, strongest kingdom the Bagrationi family had ever held.

The chroniclers didn't think much of him. They paint a young king who liked feasting and friends more than the council chamber. He kept the borders safe and talked of joining the Fifth Crusade. Then a strange army rode in from the east: the Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai, scouting ahead for Genghis Khan. In 1220 they beat George at Khunan, where he was wounded in the chest. Early in 1221 they came back and destroyed his army.

George died on 18 January 1223, aged about 30, and most accounts link his death to wounds from that fighting. He left a young son, David, but the nobles weren't ready for another child king. The crown went to George's sister.

claims.text: “Lasha” means “bright” or “illuminating” in the Abkhaz language.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle gives this explanation. Linguists aren't sure the word really works that way.

claims.text: George IV was a pleasure-loving king who neglected his duties.
claims.note: The picture comes from later Georgian chroniclers who disapproved of him. It may say more about their morals than his reign.

claims.text: He died of wounds taken fighting the Mongols.
claims.note: Several accounts tie his death to the chest wound he took at Khunan in 1220, but the sources are thin and he lived on for two years.

reigns.hook: Lasha's son is a little boy, so the crown passes to his sister Rusudan. She'll need all her mother's nerve. A shah on the run from the Mongols is heading for Georgia.

reigns.tagline: Tamar's daughter, caught between a shah and the Mongols
reigns.previously: George IV dies in 1223, his kingdom bruised by the first Mongol raid.
paragraphs: Rusudan was Tamar's daughter and, like her mother, was styled mepe, “king”. She had barely settled in when trouble arrived. Jalal al-Din, the last Khwarazmian shah, had lost his empire to the Mongols and was carving out a new one in the Caucasus. He beat the Georgians at Garni in 1225 and took Tbilisi in 1226.

The sack was brutal: churches wrecked and many people killed. The Georgian Church remembers the 100,000 martyrs of Tbilisi, told to trample icons laid on the bridge and killed for refusing. Ten years later the Mongols came in force (1236). Rusudan fled west to Kutaisi, and in the end she submitted and agreed to pay tribute.

She wanted the crown for her own son, David. Her nephew, also David, the son of George IV, stood in the way. So she sent him to her daughter's husband, the Seljuk sultan of Rum, who kept him locked up. Rusudan died in 1245 with Georgia a Mongol vassal and the succession still unsettled.

claims.text: 100,000 people of Tbilisi were killed for refusing to trample icons on the city's bridge.
claims.note: A Georgian Church tradition. The sack was real, but the number is symbolic and the details can't be checked.

claims.text: Rusudan submitted to the Mongols in 1239.
claims.note: Sources differ: some put her submission in 1239, others in 1243.

claims.text: She had her nephew David imprisoned in Rum to clear the way for her son.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle tells it this way. Her motives are the chronicler's reading, not her own words.

reigns.hook: Rusudan is dead and Georgia belongs to the Mongols. Two cousins, David the Elder and David the Younger, set off on the long road to the khan's court. Both want her crown.

reigns.title: The Two Davids
reigns.tagline: Two cousins named David, one crown, and a khan
reigns.reignEnded: David VI breaks away to the west
reigns.previously: Rusudan dies in 1245, leaving Georgia under the Mongols.
paragraphs: Rusudan died in 1245, and for a year Georgia had no king while the Mongols made up their minds. There were two Bagrationi candidates, both named David. Ulu, “the elder”, was George IV's son, freed at last from his prison in Rum. Narin, “the younger”, was Rusudan's own son. Both made the long journey across Asia to the Mongol court at Karakorum.

In 1246 the new Great Khan, Güyük, settled it by making them both kings. Ulu became David VII, the senior partner, and Narin became David VI. They ruled side by side as vassals, paying heavy tribute and sending Georgian soldiers to fight in Mongol wars, Hulagu's attack on Baghdad in 1258 among them.
It could not last. In 1259 David VI slipped away to Kutaisi in the west and set up a kingdom of his own there, later called Imereti. It was the first split of the Georgian lands that stuck.

claims.text: Both Davids were crowned at the Mongol court and ruled jointly.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian sources agree on the double kingship, though they differ on the dates.

claims.text: Georgian nobles met at Kokhtastavi to plan a rising against the Mongols, and were found out.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle tells the story. Its date, around 1245 or 1246, and how far the plot got are uncertain.

claims.text: Georgian soldiers fought in Hulagu's siege of Baghdad in 1258.
claims.note: Georgian and Armenian writers put Georgian troops there. Later tales of them leading the assault can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Narin has gone west. David VII is left alone in Tbilisi with a Mongol overlord who wants more men, more money and more wars.

reigns.tagline: The elder David, alone in the east, tries a revolt
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Co-king with his cousin David VI
reigns.cameToPower: Sole king after his cousin left
reigns.previously: In 1259 David VI breaks away and founds a western kingdom.
paragraphs: With his cousin gone, David VII ruled eastern Georgia alone under Hulagu, the Mongol Ilkhan of Iran. The demands kept coming: tax, census-takers, soldiers for distant wars. Around 1259 he snapped and raised a revolt of his own.

It failed. Mongol troops crushed the rising, and David fled west to shelter with the very cousin who had walked out on him. In 1262 he came back and made his peace with Hulagu. From then on he was a loyal vassal again, leading Georgians into the Ilkhan's wars against the rival Mongols of the Golden Horde.
David VII died in 1270, still a Mongol vassal. His heir, Demetrius, was a boy of about 11.

claims.text: After his revolt failed, David VII hid in the west with his cousin David VI.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle describes his flight. The revolt itself is dated anywhere from 1259 to 1261.

claims.text: Georgian troops fought for the Ilkhans against the Golden Horde.
claims.note: Both Persian and Georgian sources record Georgian contingents in the Ilkhan's wars of the 1260s.

reigns.hook: David VII is dead. His son Demetrius is only about 11. He will grow up into a king who must weigh one man's life against the safety of his whole country.

reigns.tagline: The king who walked to his own execution
reigns.previously: David VII dies in 1270. His young son inherits a Mongol vassal state.
paragraphs: Demetrius, Demetre in Georgian, grew up a Bagrationi king on a Mongol leash. He did the job well enough. He paid the tax, sent troops when the Ilkhans called, and spent long stretches at their court. He also got close to Buqa, the most powerful minister at the court of the Ilkhan Arghun.

In 1289 Buqa fell and was killed, accused of plotting against Arghun. Demetrius was named as one of his plotters. He could have fled into the mountains, but that would have brought a Mongol army down on Georgia. So he rode to Arghun's camp instead. He was beheaded there on 12 March 1289.
The Georgian Church made him a saint, and Georgians call him tavdadebuli, “the Self-Sacrificing”. His sons were young, and the Ilkhans now felt free to hand the crown to whoever suited them.

claims.text: Demetrius gave himself up to save Georgia from a Mongol invasion.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle says so and his journey to the camp is well attested. It's his motives that rest on the chronicle.

claims.text: He made a noble speech to his nobles before leaving for the camp.
claims.note: The chronicle gives him fine words, but they read like the writer's tribute to a saint.

claims.text: He was canonised by the Georgian Church.
claims.note: He is venerated as St Demetrius the Self-Sacrificing.

reigns.hook: With Demetrius dead, the Ilkhans treat the Georgian crown like a coat to lend out. The first man they hand it to is no son of his but a cousin from the west, Vakhtang.

reigns.tagline: A western prince on the eastern throne, by Mongol order
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Second cousin; son of David VI
reigns.previously: Demetrius II is beheaded in 1289 to spare Georgia a Mongol army.
paragraphs: Demetrius II left sons, but they were young, and the Ilkhan Arghun wanted a king he could count on. He looked west. Vakhtang was the son of David VI Narin, the cousin who had broken away to Kutaisi thirty years before. In 1289 Arghun handed him the eastern crown.

To bind him tighter, the Mongols gave him a royal bride, a Mongol princess named Oljath. Vakhtang II did what was asked of him. He paid, he obeyed, and he left almost no mark. He died in 1292 after about three years on the throne, and the crown went back to Demetrius's line.

claims.text: Vakhtang's bride Oljath belonged to the Ilkhan's own family.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle calls her a Mongol princess. Exactly whose daughter she was is not clear.

claims.text: Vakhtang was picked because Demetrius's sons were too young.
claims.note: That is the chronicle's explanation. The Ilkhan's own reasons are not recorded.

reigns.hook: Vakhtang is dead. The Ilkhans give the crown to Demetrius's eldest son, David VIII, a young man who will not stay on the leash for long.

reigns.tagline: The rebel king who held the mountains for years
reigns.cameToPower: Made king by the Ilkhan Gaykhatu
reigns.previously: Vakhtang II dies in 1292 after three quiet years.
paragraphs: David VIII was Demetrius II's eldest son, and in 1292 the Ilkhan Gaykhatu gave him his father's crown. It did not stay comfortable for long. The Ilkhanate was full of plots, and around 1297 David fell out with his masters for good. He refused to come to their court and pulled back into Mtiuleti, the high valleys north of Tbilisi.

The Mongols could not dig him out, so they made new kings instead. In 1299 the Ilkhan Ghazan crowned David's young brother George in Tbilisi. Then came another brother, Vakhtang III, and after him David's own son George. All were Bagrationi, and all ruled the lowlands while the real king sat in his mountain castles.
David never came down to beg. He died in 1311 after well over a decade of defiance, and the Mongols' kings in Tbilisi had little to show for all their crowns.

claims.text: David VIII defied the Ilkhans from his mountain strongholds for years.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian sources both describe his long revolt and the Mongol efforts to replace him.

claims.text: David broke with the Ilkhans in 1297.
claims.note: The usual date. Some accounts put the break a little later, and Georgian and Persian writers tell its cause differently.

reigns.hook: With David VIII in the hills, the Ilkhan needs a king in Tbilisi. He picks David's little brother George, a boy of about 13.

reigns.tagline: A boy king in Tbilisi while his brother holds the hills
reigns.reignEnded: Set aside for his brother Vakhtang
reigns.previously: David VIII defies the Ilkhan and retreats to the mountains.
paragraphs: George was the youngest son of the martyred Demetrius II, born around 1286. In 1299 the Ilkhan Ghazan, tired of waiting for David VIII to come down from the mountains, crowned the boy in Tbilisi in his brother's place. He was King of Tbilisi, and not much more.

He had no army of his own and no say in anything. Real power sat with the Mongol commanders on one side and his rebel brother on the other. In 1302 Ghazan swapped him for another brother, Vakhtang, and the boy was quietly set aside. Don't forget him. Sixteen years later George would be back, and he gets a card of his own.

claims.text: Ghazan crowned George in Tbilisi to replace his rebel brother.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian sources agree he was the Ilkhan's choice. His age rests on a birth year of about 1286.

claims.text: George was dropped in 1302 because Ghazan wanted a grown man on the throne.
claims.note: That is the obvious reading. The sources don't say why the Ilkhan changed his mind.

reigns.hook: George is set aside. The Ilkhan's new man in Tbilisi is another brother, Vakhtang III, and his first job is to bring David down from the mountains.

reigns.tagline: Sent by the Mongols to hunt his own brother
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of George and David VIII
reigns.previously: Ghazan drops the boy George in 1302 and looks for a grown king.
paragraphs: Vakhtang III was another son of Demetrius II. In 1302 Ghazan crowned him in place of his little brother George, and this time the Mongols expected results. The new king's task was to bring his rebel brother, David VIII, to heel.

So Vakhtang went into the mountains with Mongol troops at his side, against his own brother. The campaigns never caught David. Georgia now had two Bagrationi kings, one in Tbilisi with the Mongols and one in the hills against them, and ordinary people paid for both. Vakhtang died in 1308 with the job unfinished.

claims.text: Vakhtang led Mongol troops against his brother David in the mountains.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle describes the campaigns in outline. How hard they were fought is unclear.

claims.text: Ghazan made Vakhtang king in 1302.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian sources both place his crowning under Ghazan, who ruled until 1304.

reigns.hook: Vakhtang is dead. The Ilkhan's next choice is a child: David VIII's own son George, with his uncle, the boy king of 1299, standing behind the throne.

reigns.tagline: The little king whose uncle did the ruling
reigns.cameToPower: Named king by the Ilkhan Öljaitü
reigns.reignEnded: Died young; his uncle took over
reigns.previously: Vakhtang III dies in 1308 without catching his brother.
paragraphs: George VI was the son of the rebel David VIII, and still a child when the new Ilkhan, Öljaitü, made him king in 1308. Georgians call him Mtsire, “the Little”. Crowning the rebel's son offered David's branch of the family a way back into line.

The real ruler was his uncle George, the boy king of 1299, now a grown man and acting as regent. When David VIII died in 1311, the rising in the mountains faded and the family was whole again, at least on paper. Young George VI died in 1318, and his uncle took the crown back for himself.

claims.text: George VI reigned until 1318.
claims.note: Some historians end his reign, and his life, in 1313 or 1314, when his uncle's own reign begins in their lists. Others say 1318.

claims.text: His uncle George ruled for him as regent.
claims.note: The Georgian chronicle names the future George V as the power behind the boy's throne.

reigns.hook: The little king is dead. His uncle George, the boy the Mongols crowned and threw aside in 1302, is king again. This time he means to keep it.

reigns.tagline: The boy the Mongols discarded, back to throw them out
reigns.previously: Young George VI dies in 1318. His uncle George takes the crown back.
paragraphs: George, Giorgi in Georgian, was the youngest son of the martyred Demetrius II. The Ilkhans had made him king as a boy in 1299 and dropped him three years later. Back in charge, he played the long game. He stayed on good terms with the Mongol court and waited.

His chance came when the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id died in 1335 and the Ilkhanate fell apart. George stopped paying tribute and pushed the Mongols out. Around 1330 he had already brought western Georgia, Imereti, back under the crown. For the first time in generations there was one Georgian kingdom again, ruled by one Bagrationi king.

He put the country in order too, with new laws, including a code for the wild mountain districts. Georgians remember him as Brtskinvale, “the Brilliant”. He died in 1346 and left a restored kingdom to his son David IX.

claims.text: George V wrote the Dzeglis Deba, the law code for the mountain districts.
claims.note: The code is traditionally credited to him, but some historians think it was put together later or by others.

claims.text: He threw off Mongol rule after Abu Sa'id's death in 1335.
claims.note: The collapse of the Ilkhanate after 1335 is well documented, and Georgian sources credit George with ending the tribute.

claims.text: George V got his throne back in 1318.
claims.note: Some historians date his return to 1314, after his nephew George VI died; others to 1318.

reigns.hook: George has put Georgia back together, and his son David IX inherits it whole. But plague is on the trade roads, and out in Central Asia a lame warlord called Timur is building an empire.

reigns.tagline: He kept his father's kingdom whole through the plague years
reigns.previously: George V dies in 1346, Georgia reunited and free of the Mongols.
paragraphs: David, Davit in Georgian, inherited the best thing his father George the Brilliant had built: one Georgian kingdom, east and west, paying tribute to nobody. His job was to hold it. The Bagrationi crown had spent most of the last century on a Mongol leash, and the nobles had got used to doing as they liked.

Then came the plague. The Black Death swept along the trade roads round the Black Sea in the 1340s and reached Georgia too, emptying towns and villages. To the south the Ilkhanate was gone, and the Jalayirids who took over its western lands pressed on the border. David held on. When he died in 1360 the kingdom was still in one piece, and it passed to his son Bagrat.

claims.text: The Black Death reached Georgia early in David's reign, around 1346.
claims.note: Georgian sources mention a great plague in these years, but the exact date it arrived and the death toll are not known.

claims.text: Georgia stayed one kingdom, east and west, through David's reign.
claims.note: The chronicles show no break-up until much later; the west was still under the crown when Bagrat V succeeded.

reigns.hook: David's son Bagrat is a strong, confident king. He will need to be. Out in Central Asia a lame warlord called Timur is building an empire, and Georgia is on his road.

reigns.tagline: Timur's prisoner, who turned Timur's own army round
reigns.previously: David IX dies in 1360. Georgia is still one kingdom.
paragraphs: Bagrat V had a good start. He kept the nobles in line and married a princess of Trebizond, Anna, daughter of the Emperor Alexios III. Georgians would call him the Great. Then, in 1386, Timur came. The conqueror Europeans know as Tamerlane swept up from Iran, stormed Tbilisi that November and took Bagrat and his family prisoner.

The Georgian chronicle tells what happened next. Bagrat told Timur he would become a Muslim. Timur, pleased, gave him an army to win back his kingdom. On the way Bagrat sent word to his son George, and together they fell on Timur's troops and cut them to pieces. Timur was not a man to forgive that. He came back, and kept coming. Bagrat died in 1393 with Georgia burning.

claims.text: Bagrat pretended to convert, borrowed Timur's troops, and then destroyed them with his son George.
claims.note: This is the Georgian chronicle's story. Timur's court historians say Bagrat converted in earnest; the two accounts can't both be right.

claims.text: Timur took Tbilisi and captured Bagrat in 1386.
claims.note: Both Georgian and Timurid sources record it.

claims.text: Bagrat's second wife Anna was a daughter of Alexios III of Trebizond.
claims.note: The marriage is recorded by the Trebizond chronicler Michael Panaretos.

reigns.hook: Bagrat is dead and Timur is still coming. His son George, the man who ambushed Timur's army, now has to face the conqueror himself.

reigns.tagline: The king who hid in the mountains and would not kneel
reigns.previously: Bagrat V dies in 1393, with Timur's armies still in Georgia.
paragraphs: George VII, Giorgi in Georgian, spent his reign at war with the most feared man alive. Timur's armies came back again and again between 1394 and 1403. They burned churches and monasteries, sacked towns, killed townspeople and carried off thousands as slaves. Whole districts emptied. Georgian tradition counts eight invasions in all.

George never met Timur in open battle for long. He pulled back into the mountains and forests and kept his small army alive. In 1403, after another season of sieges, Timur offered peace and George accepted, sending gifts and agreeing to pay tribute. Timur left and died two years later. George did not get to rest. In 1407 he was killed fighting the Qara Qoyunlu, the Black Sheep Turkmen, who had moved into the gap Timur left.

claims.text: Timur invaded Georgia eight times.
claims.note: Eight is the traditional Georgian count. Historians group the campaigns differently and get different numbers.

claims.text: George made peace with Timur in 1403 by agreeing to pay tribute.
claims.note: Timur's historian Yazdi records Georgian gifts and submission; the Georgian side says little, and the exact terms are unclear.

reigns.hook: George is dead on the battlefield. His half-brother Constantine takes the crown, and the Black Sheep Turkmen and their leader Qara Yusuf are not finished with Georgia.

reigns.tagline: He chose the wrong side against the Black Sheep Turkmen
reigns.previously: George VII is killed fighting the Turkmen in 1407.
paragraphs: Constantine was Bagrat V's son by his Trebizond wife, Anna, which made him George VII's half-brother. He took over a battered kingdom and an unfinished war. The Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen, under their tough leader Qara Yusuf, were now the big power from Tabriz to the Caucasus.

Constantine looked for allies and found one in Ibrahim, the Shirvanshah, ruler of the lands on the Caspian east of Georgia. In 1412 their joint army met Qara Yusuf at Chalagan and was smashed. Constantine was captured along with his brother David and many Georgian nobles. Qara Yusuf had them put to death. The Georgian story says Constantine refused to bow to his captor to the end.

claims.text: Constantine was captured at Chalagan in 1412 and executed on Qara Yusuf's orders.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian sources agree on the defeat and his death, though not on every detail.

claims.text: He refused to bow before Qara Yusuf and was killed for it.
claims.note: This comes from Georgian tradition, which casts him as a defiant Christian king. The Turkmen side does not tell it this way.

reigns.hook: Constantine's son Alexander inherits a land of burned churches and empty villages. His whole reign will be about building it back up.

reigns.tagline: The rebuilder who shared his crown with his sons
reigns.previously: Constantine I is captured and put to death by the Turkmen in 1412.
paragraphs: Alexander inherited ruins. Timur's armies had burned towns, churches and harvests, and the Turkmen were still raiding. So he rebuilt. Churches were repaired, including, it's said, the great cathedral of Svetitskhoveli at Mtskheta, and people were settled back on empty land.

He fought the Turkmen too, and kept the kingdom in one piece. Later Georgians called him the Great, and the last king of a united Georgia free of foreign masters. In his later years he made his sons co-rulers. It looked sensible, but it gave each of them a power base of his own.
In 1442 Alexander gave up the throne and became a monk. He died a few years later, some time between August 1445 and March 1446.

claims.text: Alexander restored the cathedral of Svetitskhoveli at Mtskheta.
claims.note: Georgian tradition and the chronicles credit him with major work there, but how much of the building is his is debated.

claims.text: Making his sons co-rulers helped break the kingdom apart.
claims.note: Historians debate how much this mattered next to noble power and foreign pressure.

claims.text: He was the last king of a united Georgia free of foreign overlords.
claims.note: This is the traditional verdict of Georgian historians. It depends on how you define both “united” and “free”.

reigns.hook: Alexander is in his monk's cell. His eldest son Vakhtang IV takes the crown, but Vakhtang's brothers expect their share, and the kingdom won't stay one kingdom for long.

reigns.tagline: Four short years, then no son to follow him
reigns.previously: Alexander I gives up the throne in 1442 and becomes a monk.
paragraphs: Vakhtang IV had already been sharing the crown with his father for years. When old Alexander walked away to a monastery in 1442, Vakhtang simply carried on, now as senior king. His younger brothers had their own titles and their own ideas.

His reign was short and fairly quiet by Georgian standards. The Turkmen were still the danger in the south, and Jahan Shah of the Qara Qoyunlu raided the borderlands. Vakhtang held the line. Then in December 1446 he died, still in his early thirties, with no son. The crown passed sideways to his brother George, and with it the brothers' rivalries.

claims.text: Vakhtang was crowned co-king with his father Alexander I in 1433.
claims.note: Charters name him as king alongside his father, but historians differ on when this began and how much power it gave him.

claims.text: Jahan Shah's Turkmen invaded Georgia during Vakhtang's reign, around 1444.
claims.note: A Turkmen campaign into southern Georgia is recorded, but its date and outcome are told differently in different sources.

reigns.hook: Vakhtang is dead and childless. His brother George VIII takes the crown, and the great lords of Samtskhe are starting to act like kings themselves.

reigns.tagline: Captured by his own vassal, he built a new kingdom
reigns.previously: Vakhtang IV dies in 1446 with no son to follow him.
paragraphs: George VIII's reign is the story of Georgia falling apart. The world around it changed first. The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, and Trebizond, Georgia's old ally on the Black Sea, in 1461. Georgia was cut off from Christian Europe. In 1460 George's envoys went west to the Pope, promising to fight the Turks. No crusade came.

At home the great lords stopped obeying. The atabeg Qvarqvare of Samtskhe ran the south-west like a king. In the west a Bagrationi cousin, Bagrat, beat George's army and made himself king of Imereti in 1463. Then in 1465 Qvarqvare caught George at Paravani and took him prisoner.
When he got out, George did not try to win back the whole kingdom. He went east to Kakheti and made it a separate kingdom, ruling there as George I until his death in 1476.

claims.text: George was captured by his own vassal, the atabeg Qvarqvare of Samtskhe, at Paravani in 1465.
claims.note: Recorded in the Georgian chronicles and accepted by modern historians.

claims.text: In 1460 George's envoys travelled to the Pope and promised Georgian troops for a crusade against the Ottomans.
claims.note: The embassy, brought west by the friar Ludovico da Bologna, is recorded in Italian and Burgundian sources. The numbers of troops it promised were wildly inflated.

reigns.hook: George is a prisoner and Tbilisi has no king. Bagrat of Imereti, already crowned in the west, moves in to take the rest.

reigns.tagline: A western upstart who crowned himself king of all Georgia
reigns.previously: George VIII is captured in 1465 and heads east to Kakheti.
paragraphs: Bagrat VI was a Bagrationi from a junior branch, and he made his own luck. In 1463 he beat King George VIII's army at Chikhori with help from the atabeg of Samtskhe and had himself crowned king in Kutaisi, in the west. When George was captured two years later, Bagrat marched east, took Kartli and Tbilisi, and called himself King of Georgia.

It was a grand title for a shrinking realm. George was now king in Kakheti, the atabegs did as they pleased, and George's nephew Constantine claimed Kartli too. The Turkmen were the other threat. Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu, the White Sheep, raided deep into Georgia. Bagrat died in 1478, and Constantine moved fast.

claims.text: Uzun Hasan's Turkmen sacked Tbilisi in 1477.
claims.note: Persian and Georgian sources record Uzun Hasan's raids into Georgia, but the date and scale of the attack on Tbilisi vary.

claims.text: Bagrat won the throne of Imereti by defeating George VIII at Chikhori in 1463.
claims.note: The chronicles record the battle and his coronation at Kutaisi soon after.

reigns.hook: Bagrat is dead. His son Alexander wants the crown, but George VIII's nephew Constantine gets to Tbilisi first.

reigns.tagline: The last king of all Georgia, at least on paper
reigns.cameToPower: Took Kartli on Bagrat VI's death
reigns.previously: Bagrat VI dies in 1478, leaving the crown up for grabs.
paragraphs: Constantine II was a grandson of Alexander I, son of George VIII's brother Demetrius. He styled himself King of Georgia and spent years trying to make that true. It went badly. The atabeg of Samtskhe beat him at Aradeti, and Bagrat VI's son Alexander drove his men out of the west.

The Turkmen kept coming. Yaqub, son of Uzun Hasan, sent an army that took Tbilisi in 1488. Around 1490, worn out, Constantine accepted what everyone could see. There were now three kingdoms, Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti, plus the principality of Samtskhe. All the kings were still Bagrationi.
From then on Constantine was King of Kartli, the middle kingdom with Tbilisi. In 1501 a teenager called Ismail made himself shah in Tabriz. Constantine died in 1505.

claims.text: The atabeg of Samtskhe defeated Constantine at Aradeti in 1483.
claims.note: The battle is in the Georgian chronicles; modern references mostly date it to 1483, but the date and details are not certain.

claims.text: Constantine formally accepted the split into three kingdoms around 1490.
claims.note: The date and form of the agreement are uncertain; historians usually say around 1490 or the early 1490s.

claims.text: Turkmen sent by Yaqub took Tbilisi in 1488.
claims.note: Persian and Georgian sources record the campaign; its exact year and how long Tbilisi was held vary.

reigns.hook: Constantine's son David inherits a small kingdom wedged between two giants: Shah Ismail's new Iran and the Ottoman sultans.

reigns.tagline: He caught the king who killed his own father
reigns.previously: Constantine II dies in 1505, King of Kartli and little more.
paragraphs: David X, Davit in Georgian, ruled Kartli, the middle of the three Bagrationi kingdoms. Next door in Kakheti, King Alexander I had sent envoys to Moscow in the 1490s, the first Georgian embassy to Russia. In 1511 Alexander was murdered by his own son, George, known ever since as George the Bad.

George then went for Kartli. In 1513 David's men caught him and he died a prisoner. For a few years David held Kakheti as well. But the real danger was Safavid Iran. Shah Ismail's armies raided Kartli, and in 1522 they beat the Georgians and occupied Tbilisi. In 1525 David gave up the crown, became a monk, and died the next year.

claims.text: George the Bad of Kakheti, who had murdered his father, was captured by David's men in 1513 and died in prison.

claims.text: Safavid troops defeated David and occupied Tbilisi in 1522.
claims.note: Safavid raids on Kartli under Ismail I are well attested, but the dates of particular campaigns differ between Persian and Georgian sources.

reigns.tagline: Two years on the throne, then a monk's robe
reigns.previously: David X gives up the Kartli crown in 1525 and becomes a monk.
paragraphs: George IX, Giorgi in Georgian, was David X's brother, and he kept the Kartli throne warm for barely two years. Little is recorded of what he did as king. The Safavids were still pressing from Iran, the Ottomans from the west, and Kartli was a small, poor kingdom caught between them.

In 1527 George stepped down in favour of his nephew Luarsab, David's son, and like his brother he took monastic vows. He lived on quietly for about a dozen more years. Two Bagrationi kings of Kartli in a row had swapped the crown for a monk's cell.

claims.text: George IX abdicated in 1527 in favour of his nephew Luarsab and became a monk.
claims.note: The chronicles give the outcome, but not why he went. Some historians think the nobles pushed him out to put Luarsab on the throne.

reigns.hook: Kartli has a new king, Luarsab, David's son, and Shah Tahmasp of Iran has his eye on Tbilisi. Four Persian invasions are coming.

reigns.tagline: Four Persian invasions and a king who fought from the hills
reigns.previously: George IX gives up the Kartli throne to his nephew Luarsab in 1527.
paragraphs: Luarsab I, a Bagrationi of the Kartli line, spent almost his whole reign fighting Shah Tahmasp of Iran. The Shah came four times between 1541 and 1554. He took Tbilisi, put a garrison in it and carried off thousands of captives. Each time Luarsab slipped away into the hills and woods, waited for the Persians to go home, and came back.

In 1555 the Ottomans and Persians made peace at Amasya and simply divided Georgia between them. The west went into the Sultan's sphere, Kartli and Kakheti into the Shah's. Nobody asked the Georgians. Luarsab ignored it. In 1556 he met a Persian army at Garisi, with his son Simon leading the Georgians. Kartli's men held the field, but the king was badly wounded and died soon after.

claims.text: Shah Tahmasp invaded Kartli four times.
claims.note: Georgian and Persian chronicles both describe repeated campaigns between 1541 and 1554; four is the usual count.

claims.text: The Battle of Garisi was fought in 1556.
claims.note: Most references give 1556, but some sources date the battle, and Luarsab's death, to 1558.

claims.text: The Georgians won at Garisi, though it cost the king his life.
claims.note: That is how the Georgian chronicles tell it. Persian accounts give the battle less weight, so the outcome rests mostly on one side's story.

reigns.hook: Luarsab is dead. His son Simon is about 19 and already a battle commander. His own brother is about to sell out to the Shah.

reigns.tagline: Nine years in a Persian fortress, then twenty more at war
reigns.previously: Luarsab I falls at Garisi. His son Simon, who led the army, is king.
paragraphs: Simon (Svimon) took up his father's war, and his worst enemy was family. His brother David went over to the Shah, became a Muslim and ruled Tbilisi for Persia as Daud Khan. Simon fought him and the Persians for years. In 1569, at Partskhisi, he was captured and taken to Iran, where he spent nine years as a prisoner.

In 1578 the Ottomans invaded the Caucasus, and the Shah suddenly needed a Georgian who hated Turks. Simon was sent home to fight them. He was very good at it. He ambushed columns, besieged garrisons and won back most of Kartli. The Ottomans tried bribes and threats. Simon kept fighting.

His luck ran out in 1599, when the Ottomans caught him in battle. He was taken to Istanbul and locked in the Yedikule, the Fortress of the Seven Towers. He died there in 1611. Kartli went to his son George X, and this deck now moves east to Kakheti.

claims.text: Simon was held in the fortress of Alamut during his captivity.
claims.note: Some accounts name Alamut, the old castle of the Assassins, then used as a state prison. Others are vaguer about where he was kept.

claims.text: Simon refused to convert to Islam in Persia.
claims.note: Georgian tradition says he stood firm. Some sources say he converted outwardly to win his release, and returned to Christianity once home.

reigns.hook: Simon is in the Sultan's prison. Over in Kakheti a teenage king raised at the Shah's court is taking the throne. The Shah thinks he owns him.

reigns.tagline: The poet king who lost everything to Shah Abbas
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Grandson of Alexander II of Kakheti
reigns.previously: Simon I is lost to an Ottoman jail. In 1606 Kakheti gets a new king.
paragraphs: Teimuraz, a Bagrationi of the Kakheti line, spent part of his youth at the court of Shah Abbas I and was made king of Kakheti in 1606. Abbas expected obedience. He didn't get it. From 1614 the Shah's armies came down on Kakheti. Chroniclers count the dead in the tens of thousands and the people deported to Iran at 100,000 or more. Their descendants still live in Fereydan, in central Iran.

Teimuraz's mother Ketevan went to the Shah as a hostage. She was held for years and, at Shiraz on 13 September 1624, tortured to death for refusing to become a Muslim. The Georgian Church honours her as a saint. Two of Teimuraz's sons, also hostages, were castrated. He wrote a long poem on his mother's martyrdom.

In 1625 the Georgians struck back under Giorgi Saakadze, the Great Mouravi. They wiped out a Persian army at Martkopi, then lost at Marabda. Teimuraz ruled Kartli too from 1625 to 1633, but Persia's man Rostom pushed him out of Kartli and, in 1648, out of Kakheti as well. He ended his days a prisoner of the Shah at Astarabad in 1663.

claims.text: Ketevan was tortured with red-hot pincers before she died.
claims.note: The details come from Portuguese Augustinian friars in Shiraz who witnessed her death and took relics to Goa. Her death in 1624 is certain; the specifics rest on their account.

claims.text: Shah Abbas had Teimuraz's two hostage sons castrated.
claims.note: Georgian sources report it and it is widely repeated, but Persian chronicles say little about it.

claims.text: Saakadze later turned on Teimuraz and died in Ottoman service.
claims.note: He fell out with the king, lost at Bazaleti and fled to the Ottomans, who executed him. Motives and details vary by source.

reigns.hook: Teimuraz is beaten. Kakheti falls to Rostom, an old Bagrationi who grew up in Isfahan, prays as a Muslim and has run the Shah's capital for him.

reigns.tagline: The Shah's Muslim prefect who gave Kartli a long peace
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival Bagrationi, son of David XI
reigns.previously: Teimuraz I is driven out of Kakheti in 1648 by the Shah's man Rostom.
paragraphs: Rostom was a Bagrationi, a son of King David XI of Kartli, but he grew up in Isfahan and prayed as a Muslim. He made his career at the Safavid court and served as daruga, the Shah's prefect of Isfahan. In 1633 the Shah sent him home as King of Kartli. He was already an old man. In 1648 he beat Teimuraz I and added Kakheti, which is where this card picks him up.

Kartli under Rostom got something it hadn't had for a century: peace. Tbilisi filled up with Persian clothes, Persian titles and Persian manners. The Muslim king still protected the Georgian Church and its estates. He married Mariam Dadiani, a princess of Mingrelia, but had no son, so he adopted a young Bagrationi prince from the Mukhrani branch, Vakhtang, and made him his heir. Rostom died in 1658, in his nineties.

claims.text: Rostom, a Muslim king, protected the Georgian Church.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles and Persian sources agree on his faith and his career at Isfahan, and that the Church kept its estates under him.

claims.text: Rostom was over ninety when he died.
claims.note: His birth year is only known roughly, about 1565. If that is right he was in his nineties in 1658, but nobody wrote it down at the time.

reigns.tagline: The Mukhrani prince who planted his sons on every throne
reigns.reignEnded: Died on the road to Persia
reigns.previously: Old Rostom dies in 1658. His adopted heir Vakhtang takes Kartli.
paragraphs: Vakhtang V was the first King of Kartli from the Mukhrani branch of the Bagrationi. Before Rostom adopted him he was simply the prince of Mukhrani, a lordship near Mtskheta. To get the crown he turned Muslim, as the Shah required, and in Iran he was Shah Nawaz Khan. He married Rostom's widow, Mariam Dadiani, to keep her powerful Mingrelian family on side.

He was a smooth, ambitious operator. He got his son Archil made King of Kakheti, and for a while he even set Archil up in Imereti, the western kingdom. For a few years almost every Georgian throne was in his family's hands. He died in 1676 on a journey to Persia, leaving Kartli to his eldest son George.

claims.text: Vakhtang V put his son Archil on the thrones of both Kakheti and Imereti.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles and Lang agree that Archil ruled in both. The exact years of his spells in Imereti differ between accounts.

claims.text: Vakhtang V died at Qazvin on his way to the Shah.
claims.note: Some accounts name Qazvin; others say only that he died on the road to Persia. The place is not certain.

reigns.hook: George XI inherits Kartli. He is young, proud and tired of taking orders from Isfahan. The Shah is about to find out.

reigns.tagline: The rebel king who ended up as the Shah's top general
reigns.previously: Vakhtang V dies on the road to Persia. His son George gets Kartli.
paragraphs: George XI (Giorgi in Georgian) was the son of Vakhtang V, a Bagrationi of the Mukhrani branch. Like his father he started out as the Shah's man, with a Persian title. He didn't stay obedient. He picked fights with his neighbours and the Shah's governors and went looking for friends who might stand up to Persia.

In 1688 Isfahan lost patience. The Shah deposed him and gave Kartli to a rival Bagrationi, Erekle of the Kakheti line. George took to the hills and fought on for eight years. Then, in 1696, he made his peace. He went to Persia, became a Muslim as Gurgin Khan and turned into one of the Shah's best commanders. That road would end at Kandahar in 1709, where Afghan rebels killed him.

claims.text: George XI was killed by the Afghans of Mirwais Hotak at Kandahar in 1709.
claims.note: Persian, Georgian and European accounts agree he died there as the Shah's governor. The exact circumstances of the ambush vary.

claims.text: George XI was deposed for plotting with the Shah's enemies.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles stress his defiance; the Safavid side saw a disloyal vassal. Who he was really talking to is unclear.

reigns.hook: George XI is out. The Shah's new king of Kartli is Erekle, a Bagrationi raised in Moscow who has just become a Muslim to get the job.

reigns.tagline: Raised in Moscow, crowned in Tbilisi as the Shah's Muslim
reigns.cameToPower: Installed by the Shah as a Muslim
reigns.previously: The Shah throws out George XI in 1688. A rival gets Kartli.
paragraphs: Erekle I (Heraclius in English books) was a grandson of Teimuraz I, the poet king who had fought Shah Abbas. He spent years of his youth in Russia, at the court of the tsars in Moscow. He hoped Russia would help him win back his grandfather's Kakheti. That help never came.

So he tried Persia instead. He became a Muslim, took the name Nazar Ali Khan, and in 1688 the Shah made him King of Kartli in place of George XI. It was a messy reign. George was still out in the hills with his supporters, and the two Bagrationi kings fought over Kartli for years. In 1703 the Shah reshuffled: Erekle moved to Kakheti as its king, and George XI got Kartli back.

claims.text: Erekle I spent his youth in Moscow before turning to Persia.
claims.note: Russian records and Georgian chronicles both place him at the Russian court. How long he stayed is told differently.

claims.text: Erekle's conversion to Islam was only for the crown.
claims.note: He took it up to be made king, as several Georgian kings did. What he believed nobody can say.

reigns.hook: George XI has Kartli again, but he is far away fighting the Shah's wars. Someone has to run the kingdom. He picks his nephew Vakhtang, a young man with a passion for books.

reigns.tagline: The scholar king who gave Georgia its printing press
reigns.cameToPower: Made regent for his absent uncle
reigns.previously: Erekle I moves to Kakheti. Absent George XI gets Kartli back.
paragraphs: Vakhtang began in 1703 as regent for his uncle George XI, who was off fighting in Afghanistan. He was a builder of a different kind. In 1709 he set up Georgia's first printing press in Tbilisi, and in 1712 it printed Rustaveli's epic, The Knight in the Panther's Skin, with his own notes. He issued a law code and set scholars to gather and edit the Georgian chronicles, the Kartlis Tskhovreba.

To be confirmed as king, he had to go to Isfahan, and in 1716 he accepted Islam to get the Shah's blessing. He was king until 1724. Meanwhile he hunted for Christian allies. His uncle and tutor, the writer Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani, went all the way to Louis XIV and the pope in 1713–1716. He came back with nothing.

Then Peter the Great marched on Persia in 1722, and Vakhtang gathered his army to join him. Peter turned back. The Ottomans took Tbilisi in 1723. In 1724 Vakhtang left for Russia with a huge retinue of family and followers. He died in Astrakhan in 1737 and never saw Georgia again.

claims.text: Vakhtang's conversion to Islam was only for show.
claims.note: He needed it to get the crown, and he kept up his Christian scholarship and church work. How sincere it was is anyone's guess.

claims.text: Peter the Great promised help that never came.
claims.note: Vakhtang mustered his army for the 1722 campaign and was left exposed when Peter withdrew. Russian and Georgian sources agree.

reigns.hook: Vakhtang is gone to Russia and Ottoman troops hold Tbilisi. They need a Georgian king to front their rule, and Vakhtang's own half-brother Iese is willing.

reigns.tagline: One crown, two masters, two Muslim names
reigns.previously: Vakhtang VI leaves for Russia. The Ottomans now hold Tbilisi.
paragraphs: Iese (Jesse in English) was Vakhtang VI's half-brother and had been king once already. In 1714, while Vakhtang was stuck in Persia refusing to convert, the Shah gave Kartli to Iese, who became a Muslim as Ali Quli Khan. When Vakhtang gave in two years later, Iese was pushed aside.

Then Persia fell apart. The Ottomans took Tbilisi in 1723, and once Vakhtang left for Russia they needed a Georgian face for their rule. Iese obliged. He became their viceroy-king under another Muslim name, Mustafa Pasha. Real power sat with the Ottoman pashas and their garrison. Iese died in 1727, the last king from Vakhtang V's Mukhrani line to sit on the throne of Kartli.

claims.text: Iese changed masters and Muslim names twice to keep a crown.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles record him as Ali Quli Khan under the Shah and Mustafa Pasha under the Ottomans.

claims.text: Iese's Islam was purely political.
claims.note: Patriotic Georgian chroniclers treat him as a turncoat. Nothing he wrote survives to tell us what he believed.

reigns.hook: Iese is dead and Kartli has no king of its own. Next door in Kakheti, Constantine, a Bagrationi who serves the Shah, is still holding out against the Turks.

reigns.tagline: The Shah's man in Kakheti, holding out against the Turks
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Erekle I, of the Kakheti line
reigns.previously: Iese dies in 1727. Kartli is left with no king, only Ottoman pashas.
paragraphs: This Constantine is a different man from Constantine II of Kartli, who died in 1505. He was a son of Erekle I and had been King of Kakheti since 1722, a Muslim called Mahmad Quli Khan. In 1723 the Persians even put him over Tbilisi to replace Vakhtang VI. He held it only briefly before the Ottomans marched in.

With Iese gone in 1727, Constantine was the one Bagrationi king left standing in the east. He held on in Kakheti, raided by Lezgins from the mountains and squeezed by the Ottoman garrison in Tbilisi. In 1732 he went to meet the Ottomans under a truce. He never came back: they killed him.

claims.text: Constantine was lured to talks under a truce and murdered.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles tell it as treachery. Ottoman records give little detail, and the place and manner of his death vary.

claims.text: The Persians made Constantine master of Tbilisi in 1723.
claims.note: Georgian chronicles and Lang agree he was sent to replace Vakhtang VI and lost the city to the Ottomans the same year.

reigns.hook: Constantine is dead. His younger brother Teimuraz takes Kakheti, while to the south a Persian warlord named Nader is building an army to throw out the Turks.

reigns.tagline: Bowing to the Sultan, then to Nader, to keep a crown
reigns.cameToPower: Took Kakheti after his brother died
reigns.reignEnded: Moved to Kartli by Nader Shah
reigns.previously: The Ottomans murder Constantine of Kakheti in 1732.
paragraphs: Teimuraz II, another son of Erekle I, was a survivor. He took over Kakheti after his brother's murder and at first bowed to the Ottomans, who still held Tbilisi. He was married to Tamar, a daughter of Vakhtang VI, so the Kakheti and Mukhrani branches of the Bagrationi were tied together in his house. Their son Erekle was born in 1720.

In 1735 Nader, the warlord rebuilding Persia, drove the Ottomans out of Tbilisi, and the next year he made himself shah. Teimuraz switched masters. Nader was no rescuer. He demanded taxes, soldiers and hostages, and Georgian nobles revolted more than once. Young Erekle served in Nader's army.
In 1744 Nader paid him back. Teimuraz became King of Kartli and Erekle got Kakheti. He would rule Kartli until 1762, when he died on a visit to St Petersburg, still hunting for Russian help.

claims.text: Young Erekle went with Nader Shah to India in 1739.
claims.note: A famous tradition found in many histories. Some historians doubt it, since no contemporary record clearly puts him there.

claims.text: Nader drove the Ottomans out of Tbilisi in 1735.
claims.note: Ottoman and Persian sources agree on the handover after his victories that year.

reigns.hook: Nader has split the prize: Kartli for the father, Kakheti for the son. Erekle is 23, short, tough and restless, and he is going to spend fifty years keeping Georgia alive.

reigns.tagline: The little king who fought for fifty years and lost his city
reigns.cameToPower: Made King of Kakheti by Nader Shah
reigns.previously: Nader Shah crowns Teimuraz II in Kartli and his son Erekle in Kakheti.
paragraphs: Erekle II (often Heraclius II in English books) was small, quick and always in the saddle. Georgians called him Patara Kakhi, the Little Kakhetian. When his father died in Russia in 1762, he united Kartli and Kakheti under one Bagrationi crown. Year after year he fought off Lezgin raiders from Daghestan. In 1770 he beat the Ottomans at Aspindza, after his Russian ally, General Totleben, had marched off.

Erekle bet on Russia. By the Treaty of Georgievsk, 24 July 1783, Kartli-Kakheti became a Russian protectorate: Catherine the Great guaranteed the kingdom and the Bagrationi throne. In 1787 the Russian troops left. Agha Mohammad Khan, the new strongman of Iran, ordered Erekle to drop Russia. He refused.

In September 1795 the Persians came. At Krtsanisi, Erekle, about 75, was beaten. Tbilisi was sacked and burned. Thousands were killed, and those dragged off as slaves are usually counted at around 15,000, though figures vary. No Russian help arrived in time. Erekle died at Telavi on 11 January 1798.

claims.text: Three hundred men from Aragvi died to the last man covering the retreat at Krtsanisi.
claims.note: A cherished national tradition. Troops from the Aragvi valley did fight there, but the number and the last stand are not reliably recorded.

claims.text: Erekle was dragged from the battlefield by his grandson.
claims.note: Georgian accounts say a grandson led the old king away against his will. Which grandson and how it happened varies by telling.

claims.text: Totleben abandoned Erekle just before Aspindza.
claims.note: The Russian general quarrelled with the king and withdrew his troops. Details of the quarrel differ between Russian and Georgian accounts.

reigns.hook: Erekle is dead, and his will says the crown should pass from brother to brother. His eldest son George is sick, heavy and has other plans.

reigns.tagline: The last king, who asked the Tsar to take his kingdom
reigns.previously: Erekle II dies at Telavi, his capital in ruins and Russia far away.
paragraphs: George XII inherited a burned capital, an empty treasury and a family at war. He was in his fifties and in poor health. His stepmother, Queen Darejan, and his half-brothers pointed to Erekle's ruling that the crown should pass from brother to brother. George wanted it to go to his own son.

With Persia threatening again and his court split, George turned to Tsar Paul I. He asked him to take Kartli-Kakheti into the Russian Empire, on condition that the Bagrationi stayed on as kings. Russian troops arrived in 1799. In November 1800, alongside them, the Georgians beat an Avar and Lezgin invasion on the Iori river.
It was his last good news. George XII died in Tbilisi on 28 December 1800, the last Bagrationi king of Kartli-Kakheti. What happened to his kingdom next was decided in St Petersburg.

claims.text: George XII was very fat and too ill to rule in person for much of his reign.
claims.note: Russian envoys and Georgian writers describe his size and illnesses. How far it stopped him governing is debated.

claims.text: The victory over the Avars was won on the Iori, near Niakhura, in November 1800.
claims.note: Russian and Georgian accounts give the battle different names and dates within that month.

claims.text: George was not crowned until 1799.
claims.note: Some sources date his formal coronation to 1799, over a year after his accession. Others leave it unclear.
